## Introduction

Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is an environmentally friendly oxidant that has been extensively applied in water treatment, green synthesis, and biomedical fields1–5. Industrial production, however, is dominated by the anthraquinone oxidation process, which is energy-intensive, relies on noble metal catalysts, and generates hazardous organic byproducts6–10. These drawbacks have motivated the search for sustainable, low-impact alternatives. Photocatalytic H2O2 synthesis from water and oxygen via solar energy is an attractive option, but suffers from low selectivity, inefficient charge separation, and poor oxygen activation11–16. Current material design strategies, such as constructing donor-acceptor (D-A) frameworks, forming heterojunctions, and extending π-conjugated backbones, have improved charge separation and tuned energy levels for more efficient interfacial redox reactions17–21. However, fully conjugated architectures present inherent trade-offs: while extended π-conjugation promotes charge delocalization, it suppresses the electron localization needed for radical intermediate formation and limits the density of accessible catalytic sites22–26. Moreover, such rigid, static structures lack the capacity to adapt their morphology or interfacial environment during operation27,28.

Parallel approaches, including surface engineering, internal electric field modulation, and supramolecular assembly, have also enhanced oxygen adsorption and charge separation29–33. However, the concept of dynamic, light-triggered structural evolution that couples photophysical and morphological changes remains largely unexplored. Two-dimensional (2D) photocatalysts, with high surface-to-volume ratios, shortened charge transport pathways, and abundant exposed active sites, are attractive for H2O2 production34–36. However, strong interlayer π-π stacking often leads to aggregation and poor dispersion,37,38 whereas mechanical or chemical exfoliation methods39–42 can damage the structure or make scaling difficult43,44.

Here, we introduce a dynamic, light-responsive strategy that integrates conjugation interruption and radical-driven exfoliation to overcome these limitations. As shown in Fig. 1, this work systematically constructs a series of π-conjugated polymers incorporating redox-active anthrazoline (DADK) units and distinct bridging motifs, i.e., tetraphenylmethane (TPM), spirobifluorene (Flu), and pyrene (Py), to systematically modulate backbone conjugation topology and interlayer interactions. In particular, the TPM-DADK polymer introduces well-defined interruptions in π-conjugation via sp3-hybridized TPM nodes, which promote conjugation segmentation and electron localization of the π-conjugated backbone. This architecture promotes electron localization at the redox-active DADK sites under light irradiation, enabling the formation of long-lived ketyl radical anions (TPM-DADK•⁻). These radical anions not only function as electron reservoirs but also generate localized negative charges that induce strong electrostatic repulsion between polymer layers, effectively driving light-induced exfoliation into ultrathin 2D nanosheets under mild sonication. This dynamic exfoliation process simultaneously enhances the surface area, exposes additional catalytic sites, and optimizes charge separation and mass transport. Furthermore, the localized negative charges facilitate oxygen adsorption and activation through proton-coupled electron transfer, steering the system toward a direct two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e⁻ ORR) pathway for H2O2 generation. By systematically comparing fully conjugated (Py-DADK), partially conjugated (Flu-DADK), and conjugation-interrupted (TPM-DADK) frameworks, we decouple the effects of π-topology and steric design on charge behavior, radical stabilization, and photocatalytic performance. Overall, this study establishes a generalizable approach for designing light-adaptive polymer photocatalysts for efficient and selective solar-to-chemical energy conversion.

## Results

Synthesis and characterization of CMPs
The successful synthesis of the polymers, TPM-DADK, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK, was confirmed through comprehensive structural characterization (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1–19). Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy provided initial evidence of successful polymerization. As shown in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 9, the characteristic C-Br stretching vibrations at approximately 510 cm−1 present in the monomers (DADK-Br, TPM-Br, Flu-Br, and Py-Br) disappeared in the corresponding polymers, confirming the consumption of terminal bromo groups. The appearance of strong absorption bands at 1614 cm−1 and 1714 cm−1, corresponding to C=N and C=O vibrations, respectively, indicated the formation of imine and carbonyl groups, and the successful incorporation of redox-active DADK units into the polymer backbones.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further verified the chemical composition and bonding environment (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 10). Taking TPM-DADK as a representative example, the high-resolution C1s spectra exhibit peaks at 284.8 eV, 285.8 eV, and 287.8 eV, which are assigned to C=C, C=N, and C=O bonds, respectively, alongside a π-π* satellite peak at ~292.0 eV. The N1s and O1s spectra display signals at 398.8 eV and 532.0 eV, corresponding to pyridinic nitrogen and carbonyl oxygen, respectively. Solid-state 13C NMR spectroscopy provided further structural evidence (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 11), with characteristic signals for ketocarbonyl carbons (~187 ppm), imine carbons (~161 ppm), sp3-hybridized TPM knots (~65 ppm), and aromatic carbons (120–140 ppm). Comparable XPS and NMR results were obtained for Flu-DADK and Py-DADK.

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns indicate that all the polymers are predominantly amorphous, exhibiting only short-range structural order (Fig. 2d). The peak at 28° corresponds to an interlayer distance of ~0.31 nm, which is characteristic of π-π stacking. Compared with those of TPM-DADK, the diffraction features of Flu-DADK and Py-DADK are slightly stronger, suggesting relatively enhanced short-range ordering and interlayer interactions. The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms at 77 K revealed distinct porosity features (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 12). TPM-DADK has a predominantly microporous structure with a primary pore diameter of ~2.1 nm, along with a small fraction of larger, irregular mesoporous-macroporous voids, which is consistent with its open 3D structure. Flu-DADK and Py-DADK also display mainly microporous characteristics, with pore diameters at the boundary between the microporous and mesoporous regimes. Thermogravimetric analysis demonstrated good thermal stability (Supplementary Fig. 13), with decomposition temperatures of 526 °C and 538 °C for Flu-DADK and Py-DADK, respectively. In contrast, TPM-DADK has a lower decomposition temperature at 320 °C, which is consistent with its weaker π-π stacking and loose architecture, which are favorable for light-induced exfoliation.

The optical and electronic properties were investigated by UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra and Mott-Schottky analyses (Fig. 2f, g and Supplementary Figs. 14, 15). All the polymers presented conduction bands that were more negative than the thermodynamic requirements for both the one-step (+1.12 V vs. RHE, pH = 7.47) and two-step ORR pathways (+0.11 V vs. RHE, pH = 7.47), along with valence band maximums (VBMs) exceeding the 4e⁻ water oxidation reaction (WOR) potential (+1.88 V vs. RHE, pH = 7.47), indicating favorable energy alignment for overall H2O2 photosynthesis. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images (Fig. 2h, i and Supplementary Figs. 16–19) revealed bulk layered morphologies with lamellar organization. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) of TPM-DADK revealed lattice fringes at (0.23–1.14 nm), reflecting weak interlayer interactions conducive to light-triggered exfoliation. In contrast, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK result in smaller fringe distances and stronger crystallinity, which is consistent with enhanced π-π stacking. Collectively, these structural and morphological differences confirm the successful synthesis of the designed polymers.

Photogenerated ketyl radical anion driven exfoliation
As illustrated in Fig. 1 and Fig. 3, photogenerated electrons in polymers are captured by carbonyl groups to form ketyl radical anions under light. This electron storage process significantly alters the negative charges to the photocatalyst surface and substantially alter the local dipole moment from 0.160 Debye in the neutral DADK to 4.995 Debye in the reduced DADKH· species (Fig. 3a). The resulting electrostatic repulsion weakens π-π stacking, enabling light-induced exfoliation into nanosheets with mild sonication (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 8).

To investigate the formation of photogenerated radical species, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was employed (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 20). No detectable EPR signal was observed in the dark, whereas light irradiation induced a distinct radical signal for TPM-DADK. A carbonyl-free control polymer (TPM-DADA) exhibited a significantly weaker EPR response under identical conditions, confirming the essential role of carbonyl groups as temporary electron storage sites for radical anion formation.

To directly monitor the light-induced transformation of carbonyl groups, XPS analyses were performed (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 21). In TPM-DADK, the O1s spectrum before irradiation displays a dominant peak at 532.0 eV (C=O), which decreases under illumination, whereas a new peak emerges at 530.8 eV (C-O), providing strong evidence for the formation of ketyl radical anions and their role in photogenerated charge storage. Zeta potential measurements revealed distinct surface charge responses among the polymers. TPM-DADK, Flu-DADK, and Py-DADK exhibited pronounced negative shifts after irradiation (Fig. 3d), reflecting surface accumulation of ketyl species, whereas TPM-DADA showed negligible changes (from 17.6 to 17.1 mV, Supplementary Fig. 22). The increased negative surface potential strengthens electrostatic proton interactions, promotes hydroxyl group formation, and improves colloidal stability, demonstrating that carbonyl groups facilitate the generation of photogenerated anionic radicals and enhance surface charge modulation. Contact angle measurements further confirm enhanced hydrophilicity after irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 23 and Supplementary Movies 1–6), suggesting improved water adsorption at the photocatalyst surface.

PXRD analysis revealed the light-induced structural changes (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 24). Upon irradiation, the π-π stacking peak at ~28° was substantially attenuated, which was consistent with enhanced interlayer repulsion and exfoliation. This transformation was further corroborated by atomic force microscopy (AFM), SEM, and TEM images (Fig. 3f, g and Supplementary Figs. 25, 26), which revealed a dramatic reduction in layer thickness from ~1.25 μm to 25 nm after exfoliation. This behavior arises from its architecture with periodic conjugation breaks, introduced by the sp3-hybridized TPM nodes. Such a design promotes the localization of photogenerated electrons at carbonyl sites, while allowing for some degree of delocalization via interchain or π-π interactions. The localized electrons form ketyl radical anions that accumulate negative charges, generating electrostatic repulsion. The resulting electrostatic repulsion, combined with weakened interlayer π-π stacking and vertical extension enforced by the non-conjugated, rigid tetrahedral TPM geometry, effectively drives nanosheet exfoliation and exposes more catalytic sites. In contrast, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK feature more continuous π-conjugation and stronger interlayer stacking, which restrict electron localization and reduces electrostatic repulsion, leading to only moderate photo-thinning. Consistently, UV-vis absorption spectra of the dispersed TPM-DADK suspensions (Supplementary Fig. 27) revealed a slight blue shift after irradiation under air, reflecting weakened π-π interactions and a shortened conjugation length, thereby corroborating the efficient light-driven exfoliation of TPM-DADK. In diluted dispersed suspensions under Ar, a slight red shift was observed (Supplementary Fig. 28), which was consistent with the formation of radicals in oxygen-free conditions. These observations corroborate the efficient light-driven exfoliation of TPM-DADK and the accumulation of surface charges.

Enhanced O2 adsorption driven by photogenerated ketyl radical anions
Oxygen adsorption plays a crucial role in determining the photocatalytic performance of polymers. To evaluate the interaction between O2 and the catalysts, O2 temperature-programmed desorption (O2-TPD) experiments were conducted. As shown in Fig. 4a, compared with its analogs, TPM-DADK exhibited higher O2 uptake and stronger binding affinity. This enhancement is attributed to the formation of protonated ketyl radical anions (TPM-DADKH·) under illumination, which generate localized negative charges and create specific O-H···O interaction sites that promote electrostatic attraction and partial charge transfer with O2 molecules.

To further probe the role of ketyl radical intermediates in O2 adsorption and activation, in situ FT-IR spectroscopy was performed under O2 saturated conditions in 2-propanol (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Figs. 29–32). No oxygen-related signals were observed in the dark. Upon light irradiation, however, a distinct O-O stretching band at 950 cm−1 and broad signals ranging from 1044 to 1204 cm–1 emerged, confirming light-induced Yeager-type O2 adsorption19,45,46. Notably, the O-O signals of TPM-DADK were much stronger and more persistent (Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Fig. 29) than those of Flu-DADK and Py-DADK, highlighting the synergistic effect of protonated ketyl radical anions and the segmentally conjugated backbone. As schematically depicted in Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 30, photogenerated electrons are captured by surface carbonyl groups, forming ketyl radical anions, which, upon protonation, generate DADKH· species. These radicals retain the ability to adsorb and reduce O2 even in the dark. The presence of the O-O characteristic band at 950 cm−1 under dark conditions confirms that protonated ketyl radicals facilitate O2 adsorption. In sharp contrast, TPM-DADA, which lacks carbonyl groups, did not exhibit these O2-related spectral features or an enhanced O2 adsorption capability, further confirming the essential role of carbonyl-derived ketyl radicals in O2 activation (Supplementary Fig. 32). In contrast to fully conjugated systems, the conjugation breaks in TPM-DADK enable each polymer segment to independently store photogenerated electrons, promoting efficient and localized charge accumulation that enhances O2 adsorption and activation.

To gain further insight, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to evaluate the O2 adsorption configurations and energetics of DADK and DADKH· (Fig. 4e, Supplementary Figs. 33–37 and Supplementary Table 1). The results show that O2 preferentially binds to the O-H sites of DADKH·, forming a Yeager-type endoperoxide intermediate (O-H···O-O···H-C) at site 3. This configuration is thermodynamically favorable for the direct one-step two-electron ORR pathway to H2O2. The calculated O2 adsorption energy at the O-H site of DADKH· is more favorable than that at DADK (−1.74 vs. −0.78 kcal mol−1; Fig. 4f), corresponding to an enhancement of over 100%. Although the absolute energy difference is modest, such an increase is catalytically meaningful because slightly stronger O2 adsorption can facilitate activation while avoiding overly strong binding that impedes product desorption.

Enhanced charge separation and oxygen reduction kinetics
The efficiency of charge separation and transfer is crucial for photocatalytic performance. To elucidate the charge dynamics of the DADK-based polymers, a series of photoelectrochemical and spectroscopic analyses were performed (Fig. 5, Supplementary Figs. 38–48 and Supplementary Table 2–4).

Under photocatalytic conditions, distinct photocurrent responses were observed upon switching from Ar to air atmosphere. Notably, TPM-DADK exhibited a 60.6% decrease in the photocurrent (Fig. 5a), indicating effective electron consumption by the ORR rather than being transferred to the external circuit. In contrast, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK exhibited minimal photocurrent changes (<20%, Supplementary Fig. 38), suggesting limited electron utilization in the ORR. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) further supported these findings, with TPM-DADK showing a significantly reduced charge transfer resistance under air (Fig. 5b), which is consistent with more efficient interfacial electron transfer. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) revealed that TPM-DADK possessed the highest surface potential (ΔE=200 mV) among the three samples (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 42), reflecting enhanced charge separation. Unlike continuous conjugated systems, the strategically segmented π-framework in TPM-DADK localizes electrons within discrete domains (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 37), thereby suppressing recombination and enabling efficient charge separation and storage47. Importantly, the radicals generated in this system are not permanently isolated but remain dynamically coupled with the π-conjugated backbone. This transient interaction induces local polarization that promotes interfacial charge separation and transfer under illumination.

Strikingly, light-induced exfoliation further improved the electron transport properties of TPM-DADK. After photo-exfoliation under air, the photocurrent density increased by 480%, which was attributed to enhanced electron mobility through the thinner, more open nanosheet structure. In contrast, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK resulted in decreased photocurrents after photo-exfoliation, likely due to increased electron consumption by the ORR rather than diminished exciton generation. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence (TD-PL) spectroscopy provided further insight into charge recombination. All polymers exhibited PL quenching with increasing temperature (Fig. 5f, g and Supplementary Figs. 44, 45). Fitting the integrated PL intensity to the Arrhenius equation revealed an exciton binding energy (Eb) of 59.3 meV for TPM-DADK, which was significantly lower than that of Flu-DADK (118.5 meV) and Py-DADK (130.3 meV), confirming superior charge separation.

Furthermore, TPM-DADK displayed strong orange emission at 598 nm, which was significantly quenched upon switching the atmosphere from Ar to air (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Fig. 46), which was consistent with efficient charge transfer to O2. After self-exfoliation, the overall PL intensity became intrinsically much weaker, and the additional quenching by O2 was only slight, reflecting that most photogenerated electrons were already diverted into non-radiative transfer pathways provided by surface-bound anionic radicals. Time-resolved PL measurements of TPM-DADK further revealed that the excited-state lifetime decreased from 4.37 ns to 2.03 ns after exfoliation (Fig. 5i), indicating accelerated interfacial electron transfer and suppressed radiative recombination. The coexistence of weaker initial emission and shorter lifetimes demonstrates that the exfoliated nanosheets possess highly efficient charge separation, which promotes oxygen adsorption and reduction despite the faint luminescence. These results demonstrate that TPM-DADK combines segmented π-conjugation and dynamic exfoliation to enhance charge separation, oxygen adsorption, and interfacial electron transfer. This synergistic design optimizes the balance between charge localization and mobility, highlighting its superior photocatalytic performance for H2O2 production.

Observation of long-lived charge-separated states
To elucidate the nature and dynamics of the photoinduced intermediates, femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy was conducted under various conditions (Fig. 6, Supplementary Figs. 49–53 and Supplementary Table 5). The negative signal at approximately 380 nm, corresponding to ground-state bleaching (GSB), is essentially identical across the three samples, indicating similar ground-state absorption. In contrast, the broad positive band at 450–650 nm, assigned to excited-state absorption (ESA), varies among the samples, reflecting its higher sensitivity to charge-transfer processes. Pristine TPM-DADK under N2 exhibited weak and short-lived ESA, with the signal decaying predominantly within ~100 ps (Fig. 6a, green trace in Fig. 6f), indicating rapid excited-state relaxation and inefficient charge separation. Upon the introduction of air, the ESA signal intensified and persisted for longer durations (Fig. 5b), suggesting that molecular oxygen stabilizes photoexcited species, potentially through electron capture pathways.

Strikingly, after photo-exfoliation, the ESA of TPM-DADK was dramatically enhanced and sustained across 400–700 nm (Fig. 6c), with signals persisting beyond 4.5 ns (Fig. 6d), which is consistent with the formation of long-lived charge-separated states or radical intermediates. A spectral slice at 60 ps (Fig. 6e) revealed pronounced ESA peaks at ~480 and 600 nm, characteristic of stabilized photogenerated species enabled by structural reorganization.

Tri-exponential fitting of the fs-TA decay kinetics (Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 5) provided insights into the excited-state evolution under different conditions. Under N2, pristine TPM-DADK exhibited ultrafast decay components (τ1 = 1.07 ps, τ2 = 36.6 ps) and a short-lived third component (τ3 = 353 ps), indicative of rapid exciton deactivation and poor charge separation. In air, all lifetime components increased significantly (τ1 = 3.66 ps, τ2 = 100.8 ps, and τ3 = 1701 ps), reflecting efficient electron capture and stabilization by molecular oxygen. Strikingly, photo-exfoliated TPM-DADK in air exhibited further elongation of τ3 (1839 ps) alongside a shortened τ1 (1.48 ps), indicating rapid initial charge separation followed by prolonged stabilization of reactive intermediates. A slight reduction in τ2 (76.95 ps) suggests faster charge migration, likely due to the thinner nanosheet morphology and increased surface accessibility after exfoliation. Collectively, these results demonstrate that photo-exfoliation, combined with oxygen interaction, synergistically promotes fast charge extraction and generates long-lived reactive intermediates in TPM-DADK, contributing to its enhanced photocatalytic performance.

Photocatalytic H2O2 generation
The photocatalytic H2O2 production performance of all the polymers was evaluated under various conditions (Fig. 7, Supplementary Figs. 54–63 and Supplementary Table 6). Among the three polymers, pristine TPM-DADK exhibited superior photocatalytic performance, achieving an exceptional H2O2 production rate of 4.72 mM h–1 in pure water under O2 saturated conditions with visible light irradiation (>420 nm), substantially outperforming Flu-DADK (2.59 mM h−1) and Py-DADK (1.43 mM h−1) (Fig. 7a). Remarkably, after photo-driven exfoliation, these rates further increased, reaching 10.82 mM h−1, 4.19 mM h−1 and 2.11 mM h−1, respectively. Under ambient air, exfoliated TPM-DADK still maintained a high rate of 6.59 mM h−1 under visible light irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 56).

TPM-DADK also demonstrated excellent performance under more practical conditions. Under AM 1.5G simulated sunlight, TPM-DADK achieved a concentration-based H2O2 production rate of 14.60 mM h−1 (Fig. 7b), while the mass-normalized rate reached 17.22 mmol g−1 h−1 (Fig. 7c). It should be noted that these two metrics were obtained at different catalyst concentrations. Together, both values highlight the superior performance of TPM-DADK (Supplementary Tables 6–8).

In outdoor tests under natural sunlight and ambient conditions, the production rate remained robust at 3.99 mM h−1 (Supplementary Fig. 57). The wavelength-dependent apparent quantum yield (AQY) of the polymers aligned well with their absorption spectra (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 58). Notably, the AQY of TPM-DADK reached a peak value of 46.2% at 405 nm, highlighting its exceptional light-harvesting efficiency.

Moreover, TPM-DADK showed robust activity in real water systems, producing 13.34 mM h−1 in tap water and 13.64 mM h−1 in seawater, indicating strong environmental adaptability (Fig. 7e and Supplementary Fig. 59). Even in relatively contaminated lake water, TPM-DADK retained a high H2O2 production rate of 9.59 mM h−1, while simultaneously contributing to water purification through in situ oxidative processes.

In terms of energy conversion, TPM-DADK achieved an impressive solar-to-chemical conversion (SCC) efficiency of 3.07% under AM 1.5G simulated sunlight, surpassing most previously reported organic photocatalysts, and far exceeding the typical solar-to-biomass conversion efficiency of typical plants (~1%). Long-term recycling experiments demonstrated the excellent stability of these polymers, with negligible performance loss after at least five cycles of testing (Fig. 7f). After the photocatalytic cycle tests, the photostability of the recycled TPM-DADK was evaluated via PXRD and FT-IR analyses (Supplementary Fig. 60), confirming the good durability of the photocatalyst.

Notably, localized photoexcitation at TPM-DADK units favors selective O2 reduction to H2O2, whereas extended charge-transfer excitations across donor-acceptor interfaces in Flu-DADK and Py-DADK are generally more conducive to H2 evolution (Supplementary Figs. 62, 63). This mechanistic divergence between localized excitations and charge-transfer states is consistent with recent studies on organic semiconductor photocatalysts, where exciton localization has been shown to enhance selective two-electron oxygen reduction, whereas delocalized charge-transfer states facilitate proton reduction to H2 48,49.

Mechanistic insights into photocatalytic H2O2 generation
To elucidate the H2O2 production mechanism, a series of trapping experiments were conducted (Fig. 8a and Supplementary Fig. 64). Under O-saturated conditions, TPM-DADK achieved a H2O2 generation rate of 10.82 mM h−1 in pure water. Replacing air with Ar resulted in only trace H2O2 production, confirming that O2 was the essential reactant. The addition of KIO3 as an electron trap completely suppressed H2O2 formation, indicating that the 2e- ORR is the dominant pathway.

To assess the involvement of hydroxyl radicals (·OH) and superoxide radicals (·O2⁻), tert-butanol and p-benzoquinone (p-BQ) were employed as scavengers. Tert-butanol induced only minor inhibition (~9.7%), suggesting negligible ·OH involvement and excluding the WOR pathway. p-BQ caused slight inhibition, implying that the direct one-step 2e⁻ ORR dominated over the conventional two-step route involving ·O2⁻. Similar mechanisms were observed for Flu-DADK and Py-DADK (Supplementary Fig. 64). Nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT) assays quantified ·O2⁻ production (Fig. 8b and Supplementary Fig. 65), revealing yields of 181.03 μM h−1, 319.66 μM h−1 and 554.10 μM h−1 for TPM-DADK, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK, respectively. EPR spectroscopy with 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) as a radical trapping agent further supported these findings (Fig. 8c). TPM-DADK exhibited negligible DMPO-·O2⁻ signals compared with strong signals for DADK, confirming suppressed ·O2⁻ intermediate formation in TPM-DADK. These results demonstrate that interrupted π-conjugation in TPM-DADK enhances electron localization and ketyl radical formation, suppresses ·O2⁻ production and favors a direct 2e⁻ ORR pathway.

Koutecky-Levich analysis based on rotating disk electrode (RDE) measurements provided electron-transfer numbers (n) of 1.99, 1.80, and 1.52 for TPM-DADK, Flu-DADK, and Py-DADK, respectively (Fig. 8d and Supplementary Fig. 66), which is consistent with the highly selective 2e⁻ ORR over TPM-DADK. The rotating ring-disc electrode (RRDE) results revealed oxygen evolution via a four-electron WOR pathway for all polymers, with no 2e⁻ WOR products detected (Supplementary Figs. 67, 68). The oxygen evolution rates followed the order Py-DADK > Flu-DADK > TPM-DADK, which is consistent with the structural influence on water oxidation activity.

In-situ FT-IR spectroscopy provided molecular-level evidence for redox processes. Upon light irradiation, the C=O stretching band at 1720 cm−1 diminished, whereas new peaks at 1279 cm−1 (C-O) and 1346 cm−1 (O-H bending) emerged and later reversed in the dark (Fig. 7e and Supplementary Fig. 31). These reversible changes support the formation of protonated ketyl radical intermediates via light-induced reduction of surface ketone groups. Furthermore, a light-Ar/dark-O2 experiment (Supplementary Fig. 69) revealed that upon reintroducing O2 in the dark, approximately 36 μM H2O2 was still produced, indicating that photoinduced radical intermediates formed under illumination can continue reacting with O2 even in the absence of light. Under an O2 atmosphere, these photo-induced ketyl radicals rapidly transfer electrons to the adsorbed oxygen, whereas under Ar, they accumulate and subsequently generate H2O2 upon O2 exposure. These results underscore the critical role of long-lived ketyl intermediates in H2O2 formation.

On the basis of the experimental results and DFT calculations, a photocatalytic mechanism is proposed (Supplementary Fig. 70). Upon visible-light excitation, TPM-DADK generates photogenerated electrons and protons via water oxidation. The electrons reduce surface ketone groups to form TPM-DADKH·, which act as highly active sites for O2 activation. TPM-DADKH· enables Yeager-type dual-site adsorption of O2 at adjacent hydroxyl and benzylic positions, forming an endoperoxide-like intermediate. This structural motif enables a concerted one-step two-electron oxygen reduction pathway, in which the stored electron and the locally generated proton (either as a hydrogen atom, H·, or as H⁺+e⁻) cooperatively reduce O2 to form *H2O2. The generated *H2O2 desorbs from the surface, and TPM-DADK is regenerated, completing the catalytic cycle.

Crucially, the spatial confinement of both photogenerated electrons and protons at the active sites eliminates the need for long-range proton diffusion, accelerating proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). This precise spatiotemporal control enhances the selectivity for the 2e⁻ ORR to H2O2, while suppressing undesirable ·O2⁻ intermediates or four-electron reduction to water.

## Methods

Materials
All starting materials and solvents, unless otherwise specified, were purchased from Energy Chemical, Adamas and Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd and used without prior purification. O2 (99.999%) and Ar (99.999%) were purchased from Shaanxi Qintang New Era Gas Co., Ltd.

Characterization
1H NMR and 13C NMR spectra were recorded on a 400 MHz or a 600 MHz BRUKER spectrometer at room temperature using tetramethylsilane (TMS) as the internal standard. High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) data were collected on a Bruker maxis UHR-TOF mass spectrometer in ESI positive mode. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) measurements were carried out using a Bruker Tensor 27 spectrophotometer. X-ray single crystal diffraction data were collected on a Nonius Kappa CCD diffractometer, using MoKα radiation (λ) 0.71073 Å (graphite monochromator). The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum was recorded on an X-ray spectrometer (ESCALAB 250Xi) equipped with an Al target. The crystallinity was measured via a Bruker D8-advance diffractometer with a rotary Cu target (λ = 0.15418 nm).

UV-vis spectra and UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) was collected on a Cary 5000 (Varian) spectrometer. Emission spectra and the absolute quantum yields were recorded on a Horiba FluoroMax Plus spectrofluorometer. PL lifetimes were measured using an FLS1000 fluorescence spectrometer (Edinburgh) at room temperature. Zeta potentials were measured on a Horiba SZ-100 analyzer. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed on an EXSTAR 6000 under a flow of air by heating from room temperature to 800 oC at a rate of 10 oC min−1. Temperature programmed desorption (TPD) of O2 was measured with an AutoChem II 2920 chemisorption analyzer.

To characterize the morphology of samples, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed using a Hitachi SU8220. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) micrographs were obtained using a Hitachi TEM HT 7800 operating at 80 kV acceleration voltage. The samples were deposited onto a carbon-coated copper grid and dried. Atomic force microscopy experiments were performed on an Asylum Research Cypher VRS (Oxford instruments) atomic force microscope equipped with a Scan Asyst-HR fast scanning module and a Kelvin probe.

H2O2 photosynthesis
H2O2 photosynthesis was conducted in a 250 mL quartz reactor. Generally, 15.0 mg of photocatalyst was ultrasonically dispersed into 10.0 mL DI water. Then, the suspension was sonicated and irradiated for an hour to conduct the photo-exfoliation. After that, the reactor was illuminated by a 300 W Xe lamp (λ > 420 nm, 100 mW cm−2). The reaction was then initiated under continuous illumination while bubbling O2 to maintain an oxygen-rich environment.

Aliquots were collected every 30 min, filtered through a 0.45 μm polyethersulfone membrane, and mixed with freshly prepared Ce(SO4)2 solution. The H2O2 concentration was determined by UV-vis spectroscopy. For catalyst recycling, the photocatalyst was recovered by filtration, washed thoroughly with water, dried under vacuum at 70 °C, and reused under identical reaction conditions.

Apparent quantum yield (AQY) measurement
The apparent quantum yield (AQY) was determined under monochromatic light irradiation. The measurement was performed in deionized water (10 mL) containing 15.0 mg of photocatalyst. The light intensities at 405, 450, 550, 600 and 650 nm were measured with an optical power meter (CEL-NP2000-2, China).

The AQY (%) was calculated via the following equation:
AQY(%) = [photo H2O2 produced (mol) × 2] / [N × h × c × I × S × t × λ] × 100%

Loading photocatalyst
Solar-to-chemical conversion (SCC) efficiency measurement
The solar-to-chemical energy conversion (SCC) efficiency was tested in pure DI water without any sacrificial agents and calculated via the following equation:
SCC(%) = [ΔG × H2O2 formed (mol)] / [I × A × t] × 100%

Photoelectrochemical measurements
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements, photocurrent response measurements and Mott-Schottky measurements were performed via a CHI-660E electrochemical workstation (CHI Instruments, Shanghai, China). FTO glass coated with prepared samples, platinum wires and SCE electrodes were used as working, counter and reference electrodes, respectively.

A 300 W xenon lamp (λ > 420 nm, light intensity calibrated to 100 mW/cm2 via an optical power meter, CEL-NP2000-2, China) was used as the light source. The measurements were performed in a 0.1 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution (pH = 7.47), with potentials measured against a SCE reference electrode and converted to the RHE scale via the Nernst equation.

Rotating disk electrode (RDE) measurements
RDE measurements, employing a rotating disk electrode (glassy carbon electrode with an area of 0.196 cm2), Ag/AgCl and graphite rod electrode as the working electrode, reference electrode and counter electrode, were conducted on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai). All potentials were measured without iR compensation.

The photocatalyst ink was prepared via ultrasonic dispersion of 5 mg of photocatalyst in 500 μL of a water/ethanol/5% Nafion solution (v/v/v = 33:16:1). The working electrode (0.3 mg photocatalyst) was fabricated by drop-casting 30 μL of a catalyst ink onto its surface, followed by air-drying. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed to determine the average electron transfer number (n).

Rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE) measurements
A ring-disk electrode (PINE Corporation, USA) was used as the working electrode to measure the ORR activity. The working electrode was prepared for RDE measurements. The ORR activity was evaluated in 0.1 M Na2SO4 under an argon atmosphere at a scan rate of 10 mV s−1 and a rotation speed of 1600 rpm. Prior to the measurement, the Na2SO4 solution was purged with argon for 30 min. The potentials of the ring electrode were set to −0.23 and 0.6 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) to detect O2 or H2O2. All potentials were measured without iR compensation.

Quantitative experiment of ·O2-
To quantify the ·O2- concentration, nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT) was used as a ·O2- scavenger, as it can be reduced by ·O2- to form a purple formazan, which is insoluble in water. The photocatalytic activities of TPM-DADK, Flu-DADK and Py-DADK were evaluated in an air-saturated condition and under visible light irradiation (λ > 420 nm). For each test, 10 mg of photocatalyst was added to a 10 mL of 1 mM NBT aqueous solution within a container. After that, the dispersion was stirred in the dark for 30 min. During the irradiation, suspensions were taken from the reaction cell every 15 min, and then filtered to remove the formazan and photocatalysts. The concentration of ·O2- was determined by the degradation of NBT, measured by the absorbance change at the wavelength of 259 nm.

Theoretical calculation
All DFT calculations were performed using the Gaussian 09 software package. All molecular structures were optimized with the B3LYP-D3(BJ) functional and 6-311G* basis set, incorporating an implicit solvent model to account for solvation effects (water as solvent). Frequency calculations at the same theoretical level confirmed the optimized structures as local minima on the potential energy surface. Single-point energy calculations were conducted using the B3LYP-D3(BJ) functional with the extended 6-311+G(2d,p) basis set.

All transition state calculations were performed at the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/6-311G* level. Vibrational frequency analysis confirmed the transition state possesses a single imaginary frequency along the reaction coordinate. Intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculations verified the topological connectivity between transition states and corresponding reactants/products.

Transient absorption (TA) measurement
Transient absorption measurements were performed via a pump-probe spectrometer. A Ti:sapphire amplifier initially generated a fundamental laser pulse (wavelength: 800 nm, repetition rate: 1 kHz), which was subsequently split into two branches by a beam splitter. One branch was directed to an optical parametric amplifier (OPA) to generate pump pulses covering the 290–2600 nm range, with the pump pulses modulated at 500 Hz, and their intensity adjusted via neutral-density filter wheels. The other branch of the fundamental pulse served as the probe and was focused into a sapphire crystal to produce a white-light continuum spanning 350 nm to 1600 nm. Time delays of up to 8 ns were achieved via a motorized translation stage with a retro-reflecting mirror. Both the pump and probe beams were incident normally on the sample and spatially overlapped at the focal position. The focused spot sizes at the sample were approximately 200 μm for the probe beam and 600 μm for the pump beam.

Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements
The EPR test was carried out via EPR (Magnettech MS-5000) with a magnetic field ranging from 330 to 345 mT. 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) was selected as the paramagnetic trapping agent of ∙O2-. The measurements were carried out in CH3OH solvent with 2 mg of catalyst, exposed to irradiation with a 300 W xenon lamp (λ > 420 nm) in a Pyrex glass tube. The dispersion was purged with O2 for 15 min before light irradiation. To detect the signal of electrons in the photocatalysts, 20 mg of photocatalyst was loaded into a Pyrex glass tube and then placed in the spectrometer before and after illumination with a xenon lamp for 5 min.

In situ DRIFTS characterization
A Bruker INVENIO R FT-IR spectrometer fitted with an in situ diffuse reflectance cell provided by Harrick was used for the In Situ DRIFTS measurements. Before the measurement, it was necessary to purge with a nitrogen purge to eliminate impurities. Subsequently, water and O2 were added to the reactor in the dark until the sample reached O2 adsorption equilibrium within 1 h. Then, illumination was provided via a 300 W xenon lamp (λ > 420 nm).

Photocatalytic oxygen evolution reaction
The photocatalytic oxygen evolution reaction was performed in a Pyrex top-irradiation reacting vessel, which was connected to a glass closed gas system with a constant temperature of 5 oC (Labsolar-6A, Beijing Perfectlight). As for oxygen evolution, 5.0 mg photocatalyst was dispersed in 20 mL distilled water with 0.02 M AgNO3 as electron scavenger; 5 wt% Co co-catalyst was loaded via the in-situ photo-deposition of CoCl2. The suspension was thoroughly degassed and irradiated by a 300 W Xe lamp (full spectrum, 300 mW cm–2). The evolved gases were analyzed at a 0.5 h interval by an online gas chromatograph (GC-2002N/TFF, TCD detector, Ar carrier, 5 Å molecular sieve column).

Degradation of H2O2
Photocatalyst (10.0 mg) was suspended in H2O2 solution (2 mM, 10.0 mL) and dispersed by sonication for 30 min. The resulting mixture was bubbled Ar for 30 min in darkness, then irradiated under 300 W Xe lamp (λ > 420 nm, light intensity: 100 mW·cm–2) for 1 h. The H2O2 concentration was measured as described in Supplementary Information.

ICP-OES Analysis
The content of Pd in the polymer was determined by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, iCAP 7400, Thermo). 50 mg of TPM-DADK was digested in a mixed acid solution of HNO3/H2O2 (3:1, v/v) under heating until complete dissolution. The solution was further evaporated to a volume of less than 0.5 mL, cooled to room temperature, and then diluted to 10 mL with ultrapure water for ICP-OES measurement. The Pd concentration, determined using a calibration curve prepared from standard Pd solutions, was 0.1588 wt%.

Data availability
All other data supporting the findings of this study are available within this article and its Supplementary Information. Source data are provided in this paper.
